title: The Kessler Syndrome (where blowups multiply exponentially) applied to software
summary:
Earlier this year, inspired by a spate of supply chain attacks (like Mini Shai-Hulud-style worms, which culminated in headlines like Microsoft's Azure tools themselves being compromised), I wrote on my blog about the Kessler Syndrome, applied to software.

Ie: the rising likelihood that, because of how bad actors with agentic AI can do far more damage, more quickly with the secrets they exfiltrate from penetrated networks, we could get into a situation where essentially every network of medium or greater complexity would become permanently "tainted" (never fully clean).

Basically, can a swarm of agents 1) penetrate networks and exfiltrate secrets, 2) successfully install deeply embedded malware/rootkits, 3) move on to the next network, faster than hugops teams can rotate secrets and restore servers cleanly? For basically the entire existence of networked computers, this would have seemed a fantastical notion. But, throw in the current AI-fueled exploit discoveries and the countless servers vulnerable to RCEs across several stacks: I feel like the probability just keeps rising.

Here are excerpts from my blog post, June 10:

"'The Kessler Syndrome is a scenario where the density of objects and space debris in low Earth orbit becomes so high that collisions between them trigger a runaway chain reaction. Each crash generates thousands of new fragments, exponentially increasing the risk of further impacts and potentially rendering Earth’s orbit unusable.'

"Just counting some of the high profile examples of public repos being laced with malware lately: Microsoft just disabled 70+ of their own repos, including Azure building tools. Repos from RedHat, tanstack, axios, Mistral, UiPath, and many other lower profile targets have been hacked. The list is long, and is much longer if you count companies (not just public repos for devs) that have been bitten, including names like GitHub, Cisco, OpenAI, and more.

"...AIs or fancy new systems, probably made with AI appear to have dramatically lowered the amount of time to first utilization of stolen credentials.

"It takes too long to clean an infected system/network (and the malware is getting much smarter/vindictive about detecting its removal, further complicating things), and it takes almost no time for a batch of stolen credentials to be exploited -> new networks traversed, leading to more secrets (that likely compromise more projects, rinse and repeat).

"I think there is the very real possibility that we reach a Kessler Syndrome situation for shared/open source software, where the success of continued credential stealing campaigns permanently compromises medium, large, and even small networks, and lowers trust in shared software to a crippling degree."

In just October: > Railway - customer secrets exposure > LiteLLM - malicious PyPI + Docker releases > Zeabur - infrastructure breached > OpenCode - AI API keys exposed > OVHcloud CLI - official binaries backdoored > Rank Math PRO - malware in official plugin > TeamUpdraft - customer data compromised > ConnectWise - cloud backup identities compromised > Tensorlake - npm package infected > PingCap - alleged major breach > SubQuery - backdoored npm package > GhostAction - GitHub repos with malicious workflows > PHP - critical RCE flaws > Node.js - security flaws patched > eMudhra - certificate authority keys compromised > Tailscale - eMudhra incident

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50189771

title: Did I just spent 6 months building a product that no one wants
summary:
For the past few months, I've been building a product "Linden". Its a low latency deterministic layer for ai agents. Linden helps businesses verify AI-generated outputs before they lead to real-world actions. It evaluates AI outputs against expected schemas, trusted data, and business rules to determine whether an action should be allowed, flagged, regenerated, blocked, or sent for human review.

Linden helps businesses ensure their AI agents don't just produce convincing answers — they make decisions that align with actual business requirements, verified information, and configured limits.

I have tried cold email outreach that didn't work. Published a professional demo across multiple platforms, drove 0 signups. Now, i don't know if I just built something that serves no purpose. However, when i was building this, i did a research, looked at a lot of articles talking about the same thing. If this problem exists, then why no one willing to try it out?

title: Ask HN: Can we immortalize your startup in our Ultracapitalism game?
summary:
Hello, HN!

We've been hard at work building a company-building autobattler that's strategically deep but also doesn't take itself too seriously.

Ultracapitalism has you choose a founder and draft assets to fill out your company quarter by quarter: interns, robots, schemes, AI, private planes, and more. Asynchronous multiplayer pits your company against other real companies at the end of each fiscal year, and the goal is to dominate the market.

In addition to multiplayer, we also have PvE rivals that everyone battles against periodically, and we'd love to add a stylized version of YOUR startup/company as one of those rivals.

WHAT WE NEED FROM YOU:

- Company name

- Around 5-10 assets that define your company identity

- General CEO personality (optional; we'll design a CEO image for each company with any info we have here)

You can also use the game's Build Designer if you prefer, which gives a UI for building a company board of assets, but text here is just fine!

Web-based build designer: https://ultracapitalism.io/build-designer

WHAT IS AN ASSET?

We've got ~450 assets to choose from in the game already (you can browse them all at https://ultracapitalism.io/assets) but honestly we're still adding a ton more (shooting for ~1000 before the full game launch) so you could also come up with your own here that we'll probably add (or at least map to something equivalent).

You can also see/play the game yourself here: https://store.steampowered.com/app/5176610/Ultracapitalism/

title: Ask HN: How do you handle AI security for automated vulnerability management?
summary:
Hello World!

So I am new to the world of cybersecurity, and after some back and forth with AI, I chose to use a specific tool that was recommended for automated vulnerability detection & patching, but I think the issue I encountered is something common to all similar platforms that provide AI security fixes in 2026.

It proposed a fix to an issue labeled 'critical'. I gave the specific file and the fix to Gemini, and, it disagreed strongly.

My trust in the platform immediately degraded.

It shows in my thinking that AI security platforms for repositories are unreliable, unless you cross check every critical/high vulnerability as a human with another AI tool as well. For example, for another issue labeled 'High', the fix, I cross-checked, was correct in that case.

But that that one 'critical' issue, which turned out to be not a bug at all, and certainly not critical at all, has degraded my trust strongly in AI security platforms for automated vulnerability detection & patching. Note, to prevent confusion, with automated patching I mean automated pull requests with AI-proposed fixes, pending explicit human merging.

Now, I wonder what you guys use (instead, if at all), and how reliable your security tool(s) are, if at all, for automated vulnerability detection (& patching.)

Happy Coding!

Worldwide Wishes,

Behan
